ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Delayed cavity after stroke

An adult has a cerebral infarction after an arterial occlusion. Weeks later, the infarcted region has become a cystic cavity with loss of its original tissue architecture rather than persistent solid ghost outlines. Which process best explains this evolution?

  1. Protein denaturation that preserves cell outlines
  2. Calcium soap formation in adipose tissue
  3. Immune-complex deposition confined to vessel walls
  4. Granulomatous encapsulation of caseous debris
  5. Hydrolytic digestion of dead tissue
Answer and explanation

Hydrolytic digestion of dead tissue

Brain infarcts undergo liquefactive necrosis, in which enzymatic digestion removes the dead tissue.

Option explanations

Hydrolytic digestion of dead tissue: Brain infarcts undergo liquefactive necrosis, in which enzymatic digestion removes the dead tissue.

Protein denaturation that preserves cell outlines: Architecture-preserving denaturation characterizes coagulative necrosis.

Calcium soap formation in adipose tissue: Calcium soaps form in fat necrosis rather than an ordinary cerebral infarct.

Immune-complex deposition confined to vessel walls: Vessel-wall injury does not describe the parenchymal cavity.

Granulomatous encapsulation of caseous debris: Caseating granulomas are not the expected response to a simple ischemic stroke.
